## Assessment: Is Ro60 an established SLE autoantigen?

**Protein identity (confirmed).** Ro60 is the RNA-binding protein RO60, gene *RO60*, UniProt accession P10155, 538 amino acids. It binds misfolded non-coding RNAs, Y RNAs, and endogenous Alu retroelements that are induced by type I interferon and drive proinflammatory cytokine secretion — a biology directly relevant to lupus immunology. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P10155/entry

**Structural confidence (context).** The AlphaFold predicted structure for P10155 has a mean pLDDT of 93.3/100 ("very high" confidence), so the 3D model of the protein is well resolved. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P10155 (Note: this speaks to model reliability, not to its autoantigen status.)

**Literature evidence (supportive, with caveats).** My searches returned published papers tying Ro60 and its clinically used serological counterpart (anti-SSA/Ro) to SLE and related autoimmunity:
- A 2026 paper mapping "organ-associated autoantigenic landscapes in systemic lupus erythematosus" — places autoantigen profiling squarely within SLE. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42828094
- A 2026 study re-evaluating "Anti-SSA/SSB Antibodies as Prognostic Markers for Major Organ Damage in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus" — anti-SSA (the Ro antigen system, which includes Ro60) is treated as an SLE-relevant antibody. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42735434
- A 2026 paper on ANA fluorescence patterns and their immunological/clinical significance, the framework in which anti-Ro reactivity is clinically characterized. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42923724
- Additional papers show Ro60 as a defined autoimmune target (Ro60-reactive TCR work in Sjögren's disease: https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13651826).

**Caveats I want you to weigh.** The literature tool returned titles/abstracts-level metadata rather than extracted prevalence figures, and several top hits concern Ro52/TRIM21, Sjögren's disease, or neonatal lupus rather than Ro60 in SLE specifically. The anti-SSA/Ro antibody system is shared across SLE and Sjögren's, so some evidence is cross-disease. None of my tools returned a single definitive classification-criteria citation, so this judgment rests on converging supportive papers rather than one authoritative source. The UniProt function note establishes a strong mechanistic link (Y RNAs, type I interferon, Alu elements) but does not by itself label Ro60 an "autoantigen."

**Bottom line.** The tools returned consistent, mutually reinforcing evidence — a confirmed protein identity with lupus-relevant interferon biology, plus multiple recent papers treating the anti-SSA/Ro system (which includes Ro60) as an SLE-associated autoantibody target. The evidence supports, and nothing contradicts, Ro60 being a recognized SLE autoantigen, though much of it is at the abstract/title level and partly cross-disease with Sjögren's.

VERDICT: YES

# Assessment: Ro52 / TRIM21 as an SLE Autoantigen

## Protein identity (UniProt)
- **Ro52** is the **E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase TRIM21**, gene *TRIM21*, UniProt accession **P19474**, 475 aa. UniProt explicitly identifies it as part of the **RO/SSA ribonucleoprotein particle** — "tissue specific differences in RO/SSA proteins have been identified... The common feature of these proteins is their ability to bind HY RNAs." The RO/SSA system is the classic Ro/SSA autoantigen family. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P19474/entry

## Structural confidence (AlphaFold)
- The AlphaFold predicted structure for P19474 has a **mean pLDDT of 90.7/100 ("Very high")**, so the predicted 3D model is reliable overall. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P19474

## Published evidence (Europe PMC)
- A 2025 review directly titled **"TRIM21 regulation of IRF-mediated type I interferon signaling in systemic autoimmune diseases"** connects TRIM21 to SLE-relevant autoimmune biology. Source: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41383611
- **"Mapping organ-associated autoantigenic landscapes in systemic lupus erythematosus" (2026)** situates autoantigens within SLE. Source: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42828094
- **"TRIM Expression and Its Association With Disease Activity in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus" (2026)** links TRIM proteins to SLE disease activity. Source: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42334177
- **"Large-Scale Autoantibody Reactome Analysis... Across Different Immune-Mediated Inflammatory Diseases" (2026)** studies shared autoantibody signatures including such diseases. Source: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42608142
- A 2026 study confirms **anti-Ro52 antibodies** are a recognized, clinically measured autoantibody specificity (in that paper, in inflammatory myopathies with sicca symptoms). Source: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42344888

## Caveats (human-in-the-loop)
- UniProt confirms Ro52/TRIM21's membership in the **Ro/SSA autoantigen system**, which is a direct structural/identity link to a known autoantibody target. However, my literature searches returned papers that are **adjacent** (TRIM21 in SLE interferon biology, TRIM expression and SLE activity, anti-Ro52 as a clinical autoantibody) rather than a single paper whose title states, in isolation, "Ro52 is an SLE autoantigen." Anti-Ro52 is also prominent in Sjögren's syndrome and myositis, so it is **not specific to SLE**. An expert should review the primary papers to confirm the SLE-specific autoantibody prevalence. I did not fabricate any such specificity claim beyond what the tools returned.

## Bottom line
The tools returned convergent evidence: UniProt identifies Ro52/TRIM21 as part of the RO/SSA autoantigen system, and the literature ties TRIM21/anti-Ro52 to SLE and related systemic autoimmunity, with anti-Ro52 established as a recognized clinical autoantibody. This supports Ro52/TRIM21 being an established (if cross-disease, not SLE-exclusive) autoantigen in SLE.

VERDICT: YES

- A 2024 review, **"Ro60 — Roles in RNA Processing, Inflammation, and Rheumatic Autoimmune Diseases,"** covering the Ro/La autoantigen system in rheumatic autoimmunity. [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/39062948]

On balance, the tools returned converging evidence — a protein whose own database name is "Lupus La protein," situated in SLE autoantigen-mapping and neonatal-lupus literature — supporting that La/SSB is a recognized SLE autoantigen, while the title-level literature match is suggestive rather than explicit.

## Assessment: Sm-B/B' (gene *SNRPB*) as an SLE autoantigen

**What the tools actually returned:**

1. **Protein identity (verified).** UniProt **P14678** confirms gene *SNRPB* encodes "Small nuclear ribonucleoprotein-associated proteins B and B'" (i.e., Sm-B/B'), a **core "Sm" component of the spliceosomal U1/U2/U4/U5 snRNPs** — the Sm proteins that make up the snRNP core. [https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P14678/entry]

   - "Aberrant B cell responses as drivers of autoantibody generation and **epitope diversification in SLE** pathogenesis" (2025) [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41583477]
   - "**Mapping organ-associated autoantigenic landscapes in systemic lupus erythematosus**" (2026) [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42828094]
   - "A master **autoantigen-ome** links alternative splicing, female predilection, and COVID-19 to autoimmune diseases" (2022) [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35237749]
   - EBV molecular-mimicry papers surfaced by the SmB lupus-epitope (PPPGMRPP) query [e.g., https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42311676, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/39877080]

**Honest limitation:** None of the returned paper *titles* is a single crisp primary statement reading "SmB/B' is an established SLE autoantigen." The literature hits are largely reviews/landscape and epitope-diversification papers in which this protein appears within the SLE autoantigen context. So the support is convergent and on-topic, but contextual rather than one definitive serology paper. My own background knowledge that "anti-Sm" is a classic SLE marker is *not* something a tool returned, so I am not asserting it as a tool-cited fact.

**Bottom line for your review:** UniProt confirms P14678/*SNRPB* is the Sm-B/B' core Sm protein, and literature searches targeted at this protein returned SLE autoantigen / autoantibody-epitope papers — evidence associating it with SLE. The direct supporting literature is review/landscape-level rather than a single definitive primary paper, so I'd suggest confirming with a focused primary-serology reference before citing it as diagnostic-grade. A sensible next step would be targeted searches on specific anti-Sm assays or the James/Scofield epitope-mapping primary literature.

VERDICT: YES
